modules.name: Emergency Card
modules.description: Shows the one-row-one-move stuck card: match how you feel, do only that one thing.

modules.name: Reset Pack
modules.description: Serves one 2-minute starting strategy from the 40-strategy library, matched to the stuck state.

modules.name: Affirmations
modules.description: Rotates one ADHD-brain affirmation card per day, off by default because evidence logs beat affirmations.

modules.name: ANCHOR Method
modules.description: Runs the 7-week values-to-action workbook: daily rep, savor, mastery log, mood tick, never-miss-twice.

modules.name: Energy Map
modules.description: Tracks Magic Hours, tiers tasks Red/Amber/Green, and enforces a hard shutdown time.

modules.name: First Move
modules.description: Turns a brain dump or giant project into one verb-led sentence doable in ten minutes.

modules.name: Focus Block
modules.description: Launches an invariant 60-second start ritual, 10-3 rounds, workstation checks and body doubling.

modules.name: External Brain

modules.name: Activation Wedge

modules.name: Flight Plan

modules.name: Inbox Triage

quotes.text: You don't have to feel motivated to start — you just have to start.
A wasted morning is not a wasted day, and a wasted day is not a wasted week.
You have not failed. You've had a hard start. Those are different things.
Starting is the hardest part. Not the work itself. The starting.
ADHD brains run on interest, urgency, novelty, and challenge — not importance.
Perfectionism kills more ADHD productivity than distraction ever has. Lower the bar. Get it done.
A finished stopping point is a cold start. An unfinished one pulls you back in.
The day starts now. What happened before doesn't count.
Future-me is a stranger I'm bad at helping. But an open document I can't argue with.
What works today might not work tomorrow. That's not you being inconsistent. That's having ADHD.
Give yourself permission to stop after the tiny step. You probably won't. But the permission matters more than you'd think.
Grinding on an empty tank teaches your brain that work means suffering — which makes tomorrow's start even harder.
Pick one. Try it for two minutes. Ignore everything else until it works. That's the whole method.
Time management is a neurotypical game, and you will always lose it.
That guilt is not a character flaw. It is a design flaw. You are running premium software on incompatible hardware settings.
You are not broken, and you do not need to be repaired. You need architecture.
Stop scheduling your day by the clock. Start scheduling it by your chemistry.
For the ADHD brain, time feels more like a lava lamp.
An extra hour of sleep generates more usable output than an extra hour of work. This is not motivational fluff. It is mathematics.
Both modes look like productivity from the outside. Both modes are borrowing from tomorrow.
The entrepreneurs who last are not the ones who burn brightest. They are the ones who burn steadily.
Magic Hours are non-negotiable prime real estate.
Ten minutes feels so low-stakes that your brain barely resists starting. And for the ADHD brain, starting is eighty percent of the battle.
The breaks are not lost time. They are performance infrastructure.
Your desk is not furniture. It is a cognitive tool. Treat it like one.
Your environment is either working for your brain or against it — there is no neutral.
Do not shuffle. Consistency is the entire point.
One object. One decision. One cleaner workspace. That is momentum.
You never look at the whole elephant. You only ever look at the next bite.
Your ADHD brain works best when the horizon is close.
Done is better than perfect. Not as a vague mantra. As a literal decision rule.
The proposal that arrives on time beats the perfect one that arrives three days late.
The perfect drafts sitting in your drafts folder compound into nothing.
The ADHD brain does not typically lack the ability to prioritise. It lacks the executive function bandwidth to prioritise in the moment.
One prompt. One answer. One action.
Scattered capture is the same as no capture.
Capture must be faster than forgetting.
ADHD working memory is like a desk on a moving train: you can set things down, but the moment the scenery changes, half of them slide off the edge.
Priority is communicated through colour and position, not text.
Batching still requires you to do the executive-function-heavy work yourself. It just concentrates the drain.
Using AI to compensate for those specific impacts is not a crutch. It is a calibrated accommodation.

quotes.text: It's not laziness. It's not a character flaw. It's neurobiology.
ADHD is not a problem of knowing what to do. It's a problem of doing what you know.
Every one of these tools is passive. They wait for you to engage. They require the exact thing you don't have.
'Just start.' This is like telling someone with a broken leg to 'just walk.'
One alarm is a data point. A countdown sequence is a narrative. Your brain needs the narrative.
When everything is a priority, nothing is.
Ordering from a menu is satisfying. Completing a list is not.
Don't redirect me. Momentum is precious.
Supportive workout buddy, not disappointed teacher.
Permission granted. No guilt. Everything can wait.
Do not aggressively interrupt hyperfocus. It's one of the few ADHD superpowers. Just make sure it's pointed in the right direction.
Slow and steady beats shame and avoidance.
You just beat entropy by one item. That counts.
A 3-sentence response sent today beats a perfect paragraph never sent.
Nobody has ever said 'I wish they'd kept ignoring me.'
Curious scientist examining data, not disappointed parent reviewing a report card.
Recovery/rest (intentional downtime - this is VALID).
If you fall off, just start again. This is not failure. This is ADHD.
You don't have to restart the whole setup. You just have to read the next message it sends you.
One rail is infinitely better than zero rails.
Your brain can't distinguish between the memory of doing something and the memory of intending to do something.
'I put it somewhere safe.' Those might be the five most terrifying words in the ADHD vocabulary.
A simpler system you actually use beats a complex one you don't.
Action comes before motivation, not after.
Your problem is not a knowledge or systems deficit — it is a values–action gap.
Building the system is the avoidance behavior — it feels like progress while producing none.
Confidence comes from completing rungs, not from thinking positively.
Never miss twice — one missed day is noise; two in a row triggers the Recover protocol, not guilt.
That staleness is the mechanism, not a verdict.
That single rep is worth more than reading this twice.
Accuracy survives the ADHD 'yeah, right' reflex that kills affirmations.
Don't build another task manager that requires manual maintenance.
quotes.source: Idea: Carl's ADHD Agent (MIND design doc)

quotes.text: No shame. No 'you said you'd do this 3 days ago.' State facts, offer the next step.
quotes.source: Idea: Carl's ADHD Agent (MIND design doc)

quotes.text: Always offer ONE concrete next micro-action, not a plan.
quotes.source: Idea: Carl's ADHD Agent (MIND design doc)

quotes.text: Don't let perfect be the enemy of shipped — Phase 1 is enough to start.

tips.text: Don't 'write the report' — just open the document.
Call someone and tell them you're working for 15 minutes.
Put on a 'study with me' video or join a Focusmate room so someone else is working nearby.
Count 5-4-3-2-1 out loud and physically move toward the task on 1.
Do 10 jumping jacks or push-ups, then sit straight down and begin.
Splash cold water on your face and wrists before starting.
Tell yourself 'I only have to work on this for one hour' and set a timer; permission to stop is what gets you started.
Do 10 minutes of the thing you're dreading most; everything else gets easier afterward.
Write 'This task only needs to be good enough. B+ work is fine.' on paper and put it next to your workspace.
Move to a different room; your brain associates this place with 'stuck' right now.
Put your phone in another room — not face down on the desk, another room.
Close every browser tab except the one you need and shove the desk clutter in a drawer.
Pair the boring task with something you want — a show, fancy coffee, a saved podcast.
Change one thing about how you do the task: new pen, standing up, a completely different playlist.
Race a timer: how much can you do in 15 minutes? Try to beat yesterday.
Reframe the task as something you care about: 'clearing the path so I can do what I actually want.'
Tell someone you'll send them the work by 3pm today, then make backing out impossible.
Open a voice memo and talk through the task; transcribe later, getting it out is the hard part.
Ask 'What's the absolute minimum for this to count as done?' then only do that and stop.
Imagine yourself tomorrow morning: how will they feel if you do this now, and if you don't?
When you drift, type the next half-sentence and leave it unfinished on purpose before you go.
Keep one sticky note open; every stray thought goes there in three words, then straight back.
Say out loud 'The day starts now,' then pick the smallest useful thing for the time that's left.
Ask 'Would I say that to a friend having this exact day?' and say the friend version instead.
Before logging off, open the one file you'll need first tomorrow and leave it on screen at the exact spot.
Pick one sentence that ends the workday, write tomorrow's first task on a note, then physically close the laptop.
Eat protein with every meal, and before ADHD medication if you take it.
Protect a consistent wake time; it matters more than a consistent bedtime.
Track energy for a week, find your 2-3 sharp hours, and put the hard thing there.
Ask 'what's the version of this that takes 5 minutes?' and do that version.
Narrate what you're doing out loud like a sports commentator.
Write 'I'm stuck on X' in a message and send it to yourself or a witness.
Look at something you've finished before; you've done hard things.
Ask 'How much cognitive energy does this task require?' then 'How much do I have right now?' instead of 'What needs to get done today?'
Put Red (high-drain) work only in Magic Hours and decline 'one quick call' inside them.
Treat every Green (low-drain) task as a delete, automate or delegate candidate before it becomes a calendar candidate.
Colour-code your existing calendar Red/Amber/Green; colour is scanned faster than text.
Rate focus 1-5 when the alarm fires, never at the end of the day; retrospective ratings flatten into no clusters.
Mark each rating 'natural or forced'; a 4 that needed effort is deadline chemistry, not a Magic Hour.
Fix the stop point before the evening arrives; inside a hyperfocus wave your judgment is compromised.
Write tomorrow's top three — three, not everything — so your mind can let go, then walk away.
Ten minutes on one task, three minutes off, no screens in the break; four rounds beat a straight 52 minutes.
Same headphones, same playlist from the top, same timer, every session; boredom with the ritual is the conditioning working.
Drag one card to 'In Progress' or write the block's task on one sticky as the visual micro-commitment.
Never work in full silence; lo-fi or nature sound at coffee-shop level fills the attentional vacuum.
In a loud room, use noise-cancelling headphones plus a beta-range (14-30 Hz) binaural track, then lock the track.
Keep a fidget object within arm's reach so there is zero friction between the urge and the object.
Swap harsh overhead light for a warm 2700-3000K desk lamp plus soft light behind the monitor.
Remove one friction object from the desk right now, not later; tomorrow, another one.
Body-double once a day inside a Magic Hour: state one intention sentence, camera on, mic muted, report back.
Commit to ten minutes only at the start; enlarging the commitment removes the reason resistance collapses.
Sort the pile by cost of delay, not by what is screaming loudest.
Read the AI's sort, ignore everything but the final verb-led sentence, close the chat, set a ten-minute timer.
Write the done state as one sentence describing the end condition, not the process.
Split a project into 3-5 chunks, never fifteen, and plan no more than one or two bites ahead.
If the step has a verb like decide, think or research, it's not physical; rewrite it as open, write, send, call.
Your SOP has a typo? Ship it. Your proposal is 85% polished? Send it.
'Not yet' is only legitimate when something is missing, never when something is unpolished.
Every thought goes to one and only one capture point. Not one per device. One. Total.
Put the capture app in the phone dock, bottom row, thumb's reach, plus a lock-screen widget.
If a thought takes more than five seconds to capture the system fails; speak it, don't type it.
Process the inbox once a day in a low-energy window, 10-15 minutes, hard stop; work only from the board.
Keep the board to 3-5 columns and flag any card unmoved for three days.
Record a two-minute screen video narrating a recurring task, then ask AI to 'turn this transcript into a clean, numbered SOP.'
Batch approvals into one Green-window slot; approvals scattered through the day are the old drain with extra steps.
Name the task as a finished artifact; 'prepare for the board meeting' is a threat, not an instruction.

tips.text: Ask for 200 words of deliberately messy raw material and start crossing out what's wrong.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Ask for the three literal physical steps for the next ten minutes, not a project plan.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: When three steps is too many, ask for one task that takes exactly 60 seconds.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Flag which micro-step is the most dopamine-heavy so you have something to move toward.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Explain the problem out loud as if teaching a student; you finish holding an outline.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Spend 90% of the block in your workspace and 10% in chat; answer, paste, leave.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Say 'park this idea' then re-read the exact sentence you were writing; parking without re-entry still costs flow.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Expect the Dopamine Dip 40-60 minutes in; change the interaction (persona, sprint), not the task.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Re-reading one paragraph for ten minutes? Get three different ways to finish the thought and pick one.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Five minutes before stopping, write where you left off, the sticky point, and where the cursor goes next.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Never let a block just stop; the hyperfocus crash costs 20 minutes of 'remembering how to work' next time.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: After a block do one decompression: 60 seconds of jumping jacks, 5-4-3 senses, or wash three dishes.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Reclassify a lost morning as a System Interruption; the metric is Recovery Time, not what was lost.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Do not apologize and do not accept your own apology; absorb it and issue the next move.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Log two numbers per session, Energy 1-10 and Focus 1-10, for 14 days before analysing anything.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Score each task (+) energizing, (=) neutral, (−) draining; every (−) gets Automate, Delegate, then Batch.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Ask for a Best Case and Worst Case estimate plus three Time-Anchors where you check the clock.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Before saying yes, state the request, your top 3 and your energy X/10; if it costs over 30 minutes, name what it displaces.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Audit what you actually completed, never the plan; intentions don't move the ratio.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Surface the ratio (growth vs busywork) before a single recommendation.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Pick exactly three high-leverage tasks for next week and tag everything else Automate / Delegate / Delete.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Purge the week's screenshots and tabs into Immediate Action / Reference / Future / Noise without analysing deeply.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Set a 5-minute timer and speak every open loop into voice-to-text; don't judge the thoughts.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Permission to Rest must cite the day's actual completed work, not generic reassurance.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Front-load High Impact / Low Cognitive Tax wins; three small completions in thirty minutes signals 'we are winning today.'
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Hard deadlines due today go first; High Impact / High Tax work goes in your peak window.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Any task waiting on someone else is deprioritized; put 'send the unblocking message' in as its own item.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: At energy 3 or below, drop every high-tax item unless it has a hard deadline today.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Re-plan a collapsed day as one deferral, one batch, one timed 10-minute micro-task.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Before shutting down Sunday, open the exact document for Monday's #1 task with the cursor in place.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Attach a Dopamine Anchor to initiation: a playlist or coffee reserved for the first deep-work session only.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Name three specific inboxes you are forbidden to check until 11 AM.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Sort incoming mail into Noise / Information / Action; hide the noise but report its count.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Never write an email from scratch; give three raw bullets and edit the 90% draft.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Disable real-time email notifications and batch delivery to 9:00, 1:00 and 4:00.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Snooze only with a return trigger — a date or a place; a snooze without one is deletion with extra steps.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Five thousand unread? Move everything older than 14 days to 'Archive - Pre-AI Era' and let people follow up.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: End every synthesis with the Next 5: five specific steps for the next 48 hours, ordered by impact.

tips.text: Ask AI to map a long document first and name the three densest sections; summarize only those.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Demand a direct quote and location for every claim; if it isn't in the text, it doesn't go in the brief.
tips.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)

tips.text: Confess first: 'I am stuck. I am overwhelmed. I can't start.' The wall of awful thrives in the dark.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Ask for one instruction at a time, wait for 'done', and make the first step laughably easy.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Scanning the whole room is the overload? Ask for a hunt: 'only the blue trash, ignore everything else.'
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Say 'I am going in. Do not let me quit.' before a wall-of-awful task.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Never wrap taxes or anything serious in a game; switch to body double plus a next tiny step every five minutes.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Ask 'Is this realistic? Critique my plan.' then accept the reduced schedule without arguing.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Add ~20% to travel estimates and ~50% to task estimates until you have your own measured rate.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Before a weekend project, ask the invisible-middle questions: copy written? images? tested? how long did the last one take?
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Quarter-time check: 'Are you writing yet, or still researching? If researching, stop.'
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: After 180 minutes with slowing output you are in garbage time; stop or switch to low-load work.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: After a meeting, dump three takeaways, then a glass of water and no screen for five minutes.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Stuck in waiting mode before a 2 PM call? Set a hard 1:30 alarm, name the time budget, assign one task.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Back-chain departures: out the door at 5:00 means shoes on by 4:50 and shutdown at 4:40; alarm at 4:40.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Deferring to Friday? Load Friday's real calendar and ask 'Do you really want to sabotage Friday You?'
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Dump everything without organizing, say 'That's it.' to end, and let the sort happen after.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Tag feelings in the dump — 'call the bank and I'm terrified' — the emotion is the sequencing data.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Log loops at handoff, not completion: 'I emailed Steve. Add this to Open Loops.'
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Every Friday, each stale loop gets one binary: Keep (and schedule today) or Kill (and accept the consequence).
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Paste the link before you press buy: 'I do not press the button until the Oracle speaks.'
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Compute interest-adjusted cost, hours of labor it costs, and where it will physically live, then state your case.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Bad-day purchase? Validate the want, put it on a 72-hour Wait List, close the tab, drink water instead.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Never send a sensitive message directly; write the venom, then route it through the filter.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Grey rock rewrite: state the fact, state the boundary, request the next action, zero adjectives about them.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: A message wrecked you? Extract only sender's goal, required action and timeline; do not guess their mood.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Vent with no advice and no fixing until you type the safe word 'Cooling Down'; then mine the rant for one sentence.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Type 'Check': anxiety 1-10, focus 1-10; high anxiety plus low focus means drop the task and go to a window.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: CODE RED: Breathe. Stop. Do not email anyone yet. Do not quit. Get the facts first.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Quantify the distortion: not 'I'm bad with time' but 'I underestimate travel time by 20%.'
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Write the Do Not list first; negative constraints beat positive instructions for an EF coach.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Write If/Then trigger lines: 'If I am quiet for two days, I am likely isolating. Check in on me.'
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Phase up the scaffold: full list → three guiding questions → 'What is the very first, tiny step?'
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Occasionally disobey the AI's suggestion on purpose; the inefficient choice is the human choice.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Ask 'Does this need to be in the main thread?' and open a throwaway chat if not.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Gate a physical reward behind capture: 'no first sip of coffee until the brain dump is pasted.'
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: After a major life shift, reboot: name the new priority, swap the register, and redefine success.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Strip names before pasting: the AI needs the shape of the situation, not the entities.
tips.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)

tips.text: Never say 'just start' to yourself; acknowledge that starting is genuinely hard, then pick the three dishes.
Target the atom, not the project: 'pick up the three dishes by the sink,' not 'clean the kitchen.'
Put a time estimate in parentheses on every micro-step; the number is the affordability promise.
After every three steps ask 'Keep going or take a 5-minute break?' and honor the answer.
Keep check-ins to one or two sentences; a long check-in is the interruption it was meant to prevent.
Losing focus mid-session? Stand, stretch, three breaths, water, then set a smaller mini-goal than before.
Sprint: 15 minutes with check-ins at 5 and 10; 'only 15 minutes' is much less scary than an open session.
In flow at the 25-minute mark? Don't force the break; just note it and ask.
Three abandoned sessions in a row means stop offering sessions and ask: rest, distraction, or gentle movement?
Doom box: 15-minute timer, one item at a time, 30-second cap per item, then stop or explicitly re-up.
Caught deep-diving on one object? 'Keep, toss, or donate — trust your first instinct.'
Fifteen minutes too much today? One item from the pile; a 60-item box is gone in two months.
About to put something 'somewhere for now'? Take ten seconds and put it where it actually goes.
Low-stakes decision? Flip a coin; if the result disappoints you, that was your answer.
Morning brief under 10 lines, shape of the day first: 'a sandwich — busy bread, open middle.'
Every calendar item carries context, not a title: what it's about, what to bring, travel, what it connects to.
Name and defend the golden block, and schedule lunch inside it because you'll forget otherwise.
Build today's menu: 2-3 entrees, 4-5 sides with one doable from the couch, 2-3 real desserts.
An item on the menu three days running gets asked: order it today or take it off the menu?
Dessert must be something you genuinely enjoy; one fake dessert kills trust in the whole menu.
Finished a task? Roll a die: 1-3 acknowledgment, 4 victory lap, 5 ten guilt-free minutes, 6 jackpot.
Anchor the departure countdown to leave-by time, not event time: a 7:30 dinner 20 minutes away means T-0 is 7:10.
Each countdown rung says what to do right now: wrap up, find keys, shoes on, door check, go.
Early morning tomorrow? Start wind-down at T-90, screens off at T-30, alarm and charger check at T-15.
Meds nudge escalates every 15 minutes and the last one offers 'if you took them and forgot to tell me, just say so.'
Evening receipt: 'what got done today?' answered in three sentences max; a bookmark, not a performance review.
Log rest as a valid category; a receipt that treats downtime as waste stops getting read.
Suggest exactly one adjustment for next week. Not five. Not ten. One.
One relationship nudge per day, and it must take under 30 seconds to execute.
Late reply: acknowledge the delay in one clause, answer what they said, ask one question, stop at three sentences.
Reply to the oldest unanswered message right now with 'Hey! Sorry for the late reply. How are you?'
Breakfast by 10, lunch check at 1:30, dinner at 7; 'not hungry' still gets an apple or nuts.
Switch on one life rail, not all of them; even a morning brief plus a breakfast reminder counts.
Log 'meds', not 'I have taken my morning medication'; reduce friction to increase consistency.
Saying 'taking meds'? Check today's log first; already logged means stop and double-check.
Log the items that cause the most doubt — meds, locks, stove — not every glass of water.
Text item plus location in any format, with sub-location detail: 'safe, top shelf, behind the album.'
Before stopping, save state: working on, next step, key insight, and your mental state (flow or stuck).
Returning? Ask 'where was I?' and get the insight back before the position.
A project paused more than two weeks gets asked: still on the list, or move it to Someday?
Signed up for a free trial? Log the conversion date and set a reminder three days before it.
'I want to sign up for X' goes on a dated Considering list; check back in 48 hours.
A subscription audit ends with cancellation links, not a list; cancel the easiest one while the feeling is fresh.
Shower thoughts: dump without filtering; three duplicates beat zero captures.
Between 11 PM and 6 AM capture only: 'Got it. We'll sort this in the morning.' No conversation.
Install five core systems at setup. Not six. Then close the laptop for the day.
Week 4 must subtract something; a rollout where nothing gets removed was not audited honestly.
Every heartbeat gets quiet hours (11 PM-7 AM); the 3 AM ping is how the agent gets muted by Day 5.
Name your top three EF frictions and the exact moment you abandoned your last tool before configuring anything.
New commitment: acknowledge the enthusiasm, show the plate, offer four options, ask 'What feels right?'
More than five tasks for today? Pick the top three; the rest move to tomorrow and will still be there.
Do the rep first; motivation is an output, not a prerequisite.
Shrink the rep to its next-smallest-step: 'put the mat on the floor,' not 'stretch.'
Take 30 seconds after a completed rep to consciously register the mastery feeling.
Write one sentence of evidence in the mastery log after each rep.
Tick mood and energy 1-5 before bed; it reveals which actions move mood.
Do not expand the workbook; adding features is your avoidance tell.

tips.text: Rewrite 'I'm lazy' as 'I'm having the thought that I'm lazy' to loosen its grip.
Bridge a neglected value to an engine value: Self-care + Creativity = design a three-item wind-down as a project.
Climb the mastery ladder only when the current rung is boring-easy; a rung that fails twice gets split.
Put the loud belief on trial with facts only; the revised belief must be accurate, not positive.
Join one community that shares the value; relatedness cannot be substituted with more autonomy or competence.
Write one if-then: 'If [internal obstacle], then I will [next-smallest-step].'
Redesigned the system three times? Freeze it, delete the new version, do reps only for a week.
tips.trigger: urge to build a new system

tips.text: Treat gratitude journaling as a low-dose add-on, not a centerpiece.
Rate energy 1-5 at session start: low means admin and low-friction work, high means deep work.
tips.source: Idea: Carl's ADHD Agent (MIND design doc)

tips.text: Never accept 'I'll do it later' without a specific time; ask 'What time today?'
tips.source: Idea: Carl's ADHD Agent (MIND design doc)

tips.text: Show at most three items per message; lists overwhelm.
tips.source: Idea: Carl's ADHD Agent (MIND design doc)

tips.text: After 90 minutes on the same thing ask 'Is this the most important thing right now?'
tips.source: Idea: Carl's ADHD Agent (MIND design doc)

tips.text: Warn 30 minutes before a meeting or deadline, not only at the time.
tips.source: Idea: Carl's ADHD Agent (MIND design doc)

tips.text: Celebrate briefly and factually: 'Done. That's been open for 12 days.'
tips.source: Idea: Carl's ADHD Agent (MIND design doc)

tips.text: Re-nudge at increasing intervals (30 min, 2 h, 4 h, next day) rather than giving up after one try.

exercises.name: 5-4-3-2-1 Launch
steps: Count backwards from 5 to 1 out loud.
When you hit 1, physically move toward the task.
No thinking, no negotiating — count and go.
exercises.output: Your body is at the task with the first move begun.

exercises.name: The Brain Dump
steps: Set a timer for 5 minutes.
Write down everything in your head; don't organize.
Circle the one thing that actually has to get done today.
Put the rest somewhere you can't see it.
exercises.output: One circled item and a hidden list.

exercises.name: Worst First
exercises.trigger: a dreaded task is draining you in the background
steps: Identify the thing you're dreading most right now.
Set a 10-minute timer and do only that.
Stop when it rings; notice everything else feels easier.
exercises.output: Ten minutes of the hardest thing done.

exercises.name: The Power Hour
steps: Say: 'I only have to work on this for one hour.'
Set a one-hour timer.
When it rings you are free to stop; usually you won't.
exercises.output: One bounded hour of work and the permission to stop.

exercises.name: Re-Entry Note
exercises.trigger: about to be pulled away mid-task
steps: Type the next sentence, even half of it.
Leave it unfinished on purpose: 'Then I need to add the part about—'
When you return, finish that line first.
exercises.output: An open hook you can re-enter without a cold start.

exercises.name: The Amnesty Rule
exercises.trigger: 4pm, nothing done, guilt heavier than the task
steps: Say out loud: 'The day starts now. What happened before doesn't count.'
Pick the smallest useful thing for the time that's left.
Do that one thing.
exercises.output: A restarted day with one thing done.

exercises.name: The One Tab Rule
steps: Open the one file or tab you'll need first tomorrow.
Leave it open on screen at the exact spot you'll pick up.
Stop. Tomorrow you continue instead of deciding.
exercises.output: Tomorrow's start is half-made.

exercises.name: The Shutdown Line
exercises.trigger: end of day, work guilt bleeding into the evening
steps: Say your one sentence that ends the workday ('That's it for today').
Write tomorrow's first task on a note.
Physically close the laptop; the unfinished stuff is captured and allowed to wait.
exercises.output: A closed workday and a captured first task.

exercises.name: Magic Hours Discovery Protocol
exercises.trigger: you don't know when your brain works best
steps: For 5-7 consecutive days, set an alarm every two hours while awake.
When it fires, rate focus and energy 1-5 (1 brain fog, 5 locked in).
Note what you were doing and whether focus was natural or forced.
At week's end, find 2-3 contiguous blocks where natural 4s and 5s recur.
exercises.output: An Energy Map naming your Magic Hours and low-energy windows.

exercises.name: In-the-Zone Memory (Dopamine Win)
exercises.trigger: no energy data yet, want a first signal
steps: Think back over the past seven days.
Answer: when was the last time you felt 'in the zone' without forcing it?
Write the day, approximate time, the task, and the environment (quiet? music? alone? coffee shop?).
exercises.output: One data point for your Magic Hours — not a map yet.

exercises.name: One 10-3 Round
steps: Set a timer for ten minutes.
Work on one clearly defined task with no second tabs or phone.
Stop completely for three minutes: stand, stretch, water, no screens.
Repeat; four rounds is roughly 52 minutes.
exercises.output: One round of real output and a reset brain.

exercises.name: Momentum Trigger Stack
exercises.trigger: sitting at the desk, brain refusing to engage
steps: Physical cue: put on the headphones.
Auditory cue: press play on the same playlist, from the top, no shuffle.
Visual cue: drag one card to In Progress or write the block's task on one sticky.
Temporal cue: set a ten-minute timer.
exercises.output: A conditioned start under 60 seconds; a reflex after 2-3 weeks.

exercises.name: Friction Point Sweep
exercises.trigger: desk is a mess of distractions
steps: Find one object, mess or annoyance that pulls your attention every time you sit down.
Remove it right now — put it away, bin it, or move it out of sight.
Look at the cleared space; that is your anchor point.
Tomorrow, clear another one.
exercises.output: One cleaner anchor point on the desk.

exercises.name: Virtual Body Doubling Session
steps: Join Focusmate, Flown, or a video call with a friend.
State your intention in one sentence: 'I'm going to draft the proposal.'
Camera on, mic muted; work 25 or 50 minutes running 10-3 inside it.
Report back at the end.
exercises.output: A completed block under gentle social accountability.

exercises.name: Priority Sparring
exercises.trigger: seventeen things on the plate, frozen
steps: Paste or dictate the full brain dump; don't organize or filter it.
Ask for a sort by cost of delay, not by what feels loudest.
For the top item only, ask for the smallest physical first action under ten minutes.
Take the one verb-led sentence, close the chat, set a ten-minute timer, do it.
exercises.output: One marching order and the rest of the pile out of sight.

exercises.name: Eat the Elephant
exercises.trigger: a project too big to see the start of
steps: Write the done state in one sentence describing the end condition.
Name the 3-5 major chunks, no more.
For the first chunk only: what is the smallest physical action in the next ten minutes?
Do it, then extract the next bite; never plan more than two ahead.
exercises.output: A done state, a short chunk list, and one bite in motion.

exercises.name: Hard Shutdown Ritual
exercises.trigger: working late, riding a wave or sitting idle at the desk
steps: Reach the fixed, pre-set stop point regardless of what is finished.
Close the laptop.
Write tomorrow's top three tasks in your External Brain.
Walk away.
exercises.output: Tomorrow's Magic Hours protected.

exercises.name: Tier the List Red/Amber/Green
steps: For each task ask: how much cognitive energy does this require?
Red = deep focus, creative, high stakes; Amber = emails, calls, check-ins; Green = filing, admin, scheduling.
Place Red only in Magic Hours, Amber mid-energy, Green lowest-energy or delete/automate.
If Red exceeds available Magic Hours, name what doesn't fit — don't invent a window.
exercises.output: A placed task list with capacity conflicts visible.

exercises.name: Zero-Draft
exercises.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
steps: Ask: 'write a Zero-Draft of the first section — messy, basic, 200 words of raw material.'
Say out loud it is meant to be bad.
Paste it in and start crossing out what's wrong; let the corrective impulse fire.
exercises.output: A page that exists and a task converted from creating to editing.

exercises.name: First Physical Move
exercises.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
steps: Ask for the three literal physical steps for the next ten minutes.
Reject any step with decide, research, think or plan in it.
Do step one; report back before taking step two.
exercises.output: Three mechanical moves and the project's emotional weight bypassed.

exercises.name: Atomization (Act as my Prefrontal Cortex)
exercises.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
steps: Ask for the task broken into 5-minute micro-steps.
Each step gets a low-friction instruction ('open the browser tab,' not 'research competitors').
Ask which step is the most dopamine-heavy and look forward to it.
exercises.output: A short chain of micro-steps with a reward step flagged.

exercises.name: Rubber Ducking
exercises.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
exercises.trigger: can't explain what the thing even is
steps: Stop trying to write it down.
Explain the problem out loud as if teaching a student: 'here is the mess of ideas I have…'
Let the listener synthesize as you talk.
exercises.output: An outline you produced by talking.

exercises.name: Gatekeeper Mandate Setup
exercises.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
exercises.trigger: want to be held on track for 60-90 minutes
steps: State the Primary Objective as a finished artifact.
State the Permitted Scope; everything else is a tangent to be saved, not answered.
State the duration and wall-clock end time.
Agree: one-sentence status every 20 minutes; no apologies, just redirects.
exercises.output: A digital container for one block of focus.

exercises.name: Breadcrumb Note (Context Save)
exercises.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
steps: Brain-dump what you just finished and what you were about to do.
Write three lines: Where we left off / The 'Sticky' Point / The Next Move.
Make The Next Move a literal cursor position or physical action.
Put the note where you'll see it next session.
exercises.output: A three-line re-entry point that starts the next session in editing mode.

exercises.name: Emergency Reset (1% More in Control)
exercises.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
exercises.trigger: lost three hours, shame and low energy
steps: Report it flatly; no apology.
Say 'Forget the previous plan. We are starting at zero.'
Do one physical reset: close all 50 tabs, stretch 30 seconds, or drink a glass of water.
Then one single low-stakes task to re-engage.
exercises.output: Recovery begun; the day reclassified as a System Interruption.

exercises.name: Time-Audit
exercises.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
exercises.trigger: about to commit to a task estimate
steps: State the task and your known distraction pattern.
Get a realistic Best Case and Worst Case duration.
Set three Time-Anchors — points in the task where you check the clock.
exercises.output: A calibrated estimate with rabbit-hole checkpoints.

exercises.name: Commitment Filter
exercises.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
exercises.trigger: someone just asked you to take something on
steps: Write the request, your current top 3 priorities, and energy X/10.
Ask: if this takes more than 30 minutes, what does it do to the top 3?
Verdict: accept, decline, or defer.
If declining, draft the polite reply citing the conflicting priority, not your capacity.
exercises.output: A verdict and a sendable decline if needed.

exercises.name: Roadmap vs. Reality Audit
exercises.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
exercises.trigger: end of week, want the brutal truth
steps: List every task actually completed this week plus your goal document.
Classify each as Empire Building (moves the goal) or Maintenance.
Calculate the ratio as a percentage.
Name the #1 distraction to cut next week; then pick the Vital Three.
exercises.output: A ratio, a verdict, and one cut.

exercises.name: Mind Sweep
exercises.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
steps: Set a 5-minute timer.
Speak everything into voice-to-text: worries, ideas, errands; don't judge.
Ask for hidden tasks to be extracted to a Pending list.
exercises.output: Open loops out of your head and into a list.

exercises.name: Monday Launchpad + Open Loop Pre-Load
exercises.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
steps: Write the Prime Directive: the one outcome for Monday.
Write the First Move: a physical action on a named file, under two minutes.
Name three 'urgent' inboxes forbidden until 11 AM.
Open the exact document for the #1 task, cursor in place, and name your Dopamine Anchor.
exercises.output: A mission briefing and a pre-loaded Monday start.

exercises.name: Micro-Slicer Session
exercises.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
exercises.trigger: paralyzed by a room or task
steps: Confess: 'I am stuck. I am overwhelmed. I can't start.'
Take one instruction: 'Pick up exactly three pieces of trash. Throw them away. Tell me when you are back.'
Report 'Done'; take the next slice.
If a slice stalls, halve it; if scanning is the problem, switch to a hunt.
exercises.output: Physical motion and a task shrinking one slice at a time.

exercises.name: Sensory Slicing (Give Me a Hunt)
exercises.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
exercises.trigger: even 'pick up trash' needs too much scanning
steps: Pick one attribute: a colour, an object class, a container, a sender.
Hunt only that: 'find all the blue trash; ignore the red, ignore the papers.'
When that attribute is cleared, pick the next.
exercises.output: Clutter turned into a Where's Waldo puzzle and partly cleared.

exercises.name: Reality Check
exercises.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
exercises.trigger: 'I can do these five things in an hour'
steps: State the list and ask: 'Is this realistic? Critique my plan.'
Accept the duration evidence ('task #3 usually takes you 45 minutes alone').
Pick one major and one minor task; answer 'Which is the priority?'
Fight the urge to argue.
exercises.output: A reduced, honest schedule.

exercises.name: Transition Buffer
exercises.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
exercises.trigger: just finished one thing, can't start the next
steps: Dump the three immediate takeaways from what you just finished.
Get a glass of water.
No screen for five minutes.
Then start the next task.
exercises.output: Working-memory residue cleared and permission to buffer.

exercises.name: Waiting Mode Antidote
exercises.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
exercises.trigger: an appointment later is burning the hours before it
steps: Set a hard alarm for 30 minutes before the appointment.
Say out loud: the alarm is watching the clock, not me.
Name the time budget: 'we have exactly three hours.'
Assign one task to that budget and start it.
exercises.output: Vigilance handed to the clock and a block reclaimed.

exercises.name: Departure Back-Chain
exercises.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
steps: Define T as walking out the door.
Shoes on and bag packed by T-10.
Shutdown sequence starts at T-20.
Set the alarm at T-20, never at T.
exercises.output: An alarm on the earliest step instead of the departure time.

exercises.name: Future-Self Simulation
exercises.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
steps: Load Friday's real commitments.
Name the slot actually left and your typical energy in it.
State the predicted outcome plainly.
Ask: 'Do you really want to sabotage Friday You?'
exercises.output: A concrete picture of the deferral's cost and a now-as-gift reframe.

exercises.name: Dump & Sort (Ingestion Mode)
exercises.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
steps: Declare Ingestion Mode; no interruptions until the phrase 'That's it.'
Dump everything by voice or text, tagging feelings ('and I'm terrified').
Say 'That's it.'
Receive one table with every item in a bucket; use emotional tags to pick the first move.
exercises.output: Every item captured and sorted; a first move proposed.

exercises.name: Graveyard of Good Intentions
exercises.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
steps: List every open loop with how long it has sat and what has actually happened.
For each: Keep (and schedule a specific action today) or Kill (and accept the named consequence)?
Actually delete the killed items and say so.
Count what you are no longer carrying.
exercises.output: A shorter loop list and the anxiety hum reduced.

exercises.name: Autopsy of a Bad Week
exercises.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
exercises.trigger: why do I keep doing this
steps: Pick a recent calendar week where everything went wrong.
Narrate it day by day, including feelings and friction points, not just events.
Label each incident mechanically: Decision Paralysis, Time Blindness, Context Switching, People Pleasing…
Distill each into one declarative, quantified Bio-File line.
exercises.output: A table of incident → pattern → rule.

exercises.name: First Step Generator
steps: Get ONE action under five minutes, absurdly specific: 'open the document and type the title.'
Do it; confirm.
Get the next tiny step; continue until momentum or until you say stop.
If a step feels too big, break it smaller.
exercises.output: A started task with momentum building.

exercises.name: Momentum Chain
exercises.trigger: a multi-part physical job like a messy office
steps: Break the job into 5-8 micro-steps of 2-5 minutes, but see only the first.
Do step one (e.g. 'clear everything off the desk onto the floor, 2 min').
Confirm, get the next; brief celebration between steps.
After every three: keep going or take a 5-minute break?
exercises.output: A finished room in under 20 minutes, or an honored break.

exercises.name: Doom Box Sprint
exercises.trigger: the pile that gives you a twinge of guilt
steps: Set a 15-minute timer; you are not doing the whole thing today.
Pick up the first item and name it.
Categorize fast: trash / keep (has a home) / keep (homeless) / action needed / sentimental (3 seconds) / donate.
At the timer: another 15 or call it a win? Log items sorted.
exercises.output: X items sorted and a logged count.

exercises.name: Decision Helper
steps: List the options simply: A, B, C (three max).
For each: best thing that happens? worst thing?
Take a committed recommendation, then check your gut.
Still stuck: 60 seconds to pick or a coin flips; disappointment at the result is your answer.
exercises.output: A decision made or a coin-flip diagnostic.

exercises.name: Build Today's Menu
steps: ENTREES (pick 1): 2-3 substantial 30+ minute items.
SIDES (pick 2): 4-5 quick wins under 15 minutes, one doable from the couch.
DESSERT (pick 1): 2-3 things you genuinely enjoy.
Order one from each course; that's your day, not the whole list.
exercises.output: A three-course menu and one order placed.

exercises.name: Departure Countdown Ladder
exercises.trigger: an event that needs you out the door
steps: Compute leave-by time: event time minus travel minus 15 minutes transition.
T-45: wrap up; T-30: save work, where are keys and wallet?; T-15: shoes, stuff, water bottle.
T-5: at the door, phone/wallet/keys check; T-0: go.
T+5: 'did you make it out the door? No judgment, just checking.'
exercises.output: A six-rung ladder that externalizes the whole transition.

exercises.name: Evening Quick Receipt
steps: Ask: 'Quick daily receipt — what got done today?'
Summarize and celebrate in three sentences max.
Nothing to report? 'No receipt tonight? That's fine. Rest up — tomorrow's a new one.'
exercises.output: A bookmark on the day, not a performance review.

exercises.name: Weekly Attention Report
steps: Wins column: completions and progress, even small ones.
Where attention went (~hours): productive focus / necessary maintenance / recovery (valid) / rabbit holes / escape.
Patterns: most productive hours, triggers before escape, lost days and what preceded them.
One curiosity question (either answer is fine), then ONE adjustment for next week.
exercises.output: A curious-scientist report and one proposed change.

exercises.name: Save State
exercises.trigger: about to stop or switch projects
steps: What were you working on specifically?
What was your next planned step?
Any key insights or decisions to remember?
Note your mental state: flow, stuck, frustrated, excited.
exercises.output: A save state you can restore with 'where was I?'

exercises.name: Subscription Audit
exercises.trigger: first setup or monthly money review
steps: Search 12 months of email for receipt, subscription, renewal, billing, trial, auto-renew.
Master list: service, monthly cost (annual converted), last real use, KEEPER / REVIEW / CANCEL.
Total the monthly spend; anything untouched 30+ days is CANCEL.
Find the actual cancellation link for each CANCEL and cancel the easiest one now.
exercises.output: A totalled list and at least one cancellation done.

exercises.name: Object Seeding Sweep
steps: Say: 'Let's do an object sweep. I'm going to tell you where things are as I walk through.'
Walk room by room naming item plus sub-location.
Start with passport, spare keys, important documents, emergency supplies, your most-lost item.
Confirm the batch at the end.
exercises.output: A seeded Physical Items log that can answer 'where are my…?'

exercises.name: Values-Alignment Tracker
steps: List your ranked values.
For each, mark current action honestly: often / rarely.
Mark whether loved ones share it: low / moderate.
Circle the two lowest-alignment values that matter most; the top-ranked, least-acted one is the target.
exercises.output: A measurable values-action gap and a target value.

exercises.name: Defusion Drill
steps: Write three recurring self-criticisms.
Rewrite each as 'I'm having the thought that…'
Notice the thought is now an object, not an order.
exercises.output: Three defused thoughts with less behavioral grip.

exercises.name: Relatedness Map
steps: For each value, name any person or community that shares it, or write 'none yet'.
Mark the values running with zero social reinforcement.
Pick one community of interest to source relatedness deliberately.
exercises.output: A map of where values are socially isolated and one place to fix it.

exercises.name: Micro-Action Menu of 8
steps: Using the interest-bridging table, write 8 micro-actions for the target value, each ten minutes or less.
Bridge each to an engine value (creativity, knowledge, courage, competition).
Keep the menu visible; pick one per day without deciding fresh.
exercises.output: A menu that removes daily decision cost.

exercises.name: Next-Smallest-Step Rewrite
steps: Take each menu item.
Rewrite it as its next-smallest-step: not 'stretch' but 'put the mat on the floor.'
Add one novelty injection: new place, new time, or body-double one rep.
exercises.output: Reps small enough to survive your worst day.

exercises.name: Mastery Ladder
steps: Pick one neglected value.
Write 5 rungs, each a task you are ~80% sure you can complete (5 min walk → 10 min → 10+5 mobility → 15 min x3 → 20 min designed session).
Climb only when the current rung is boring-easy; split any rung that fails twice.
Log each completed rung as one line of evidence.
exercises.output: A ladder and a mastery log that counters 'I can't stick to anything.'

exercises.name: Limiting-Belief Evidence Log
steps: Write the belief and rate its strength 0-100.
List evidence FOR, facts only.
List evidence AGAINST, facts only, including your mastery log.
Write a revised, more accurate belief and re-rate it; if it won't drop, make it more accurate, not more positive.
exercises.output: A court-case verdict on the belief, with a new strength number.

exercises.name: Purpose Sentence Sequence
steps: List activities that are meaningful to you from acted-on values.
For each, name who or what beyond you it could serve.
Draft: 'I want to [action] so that [beyond-self consequence].'
Stress-test: a commitment or a dreamer's wish? Attach one weekly recurring action and one community.
exercises.output: One purpose sentence with a weekly action tied to it.

exercises.name: WOOP Obstacle Sheet
steps: Wish: a challenging but achievable value goal.
Outcome: picture the best result; note benefits of doing and costs of not doing.
Obstacle: the internal state that actually stops you.
Plan: 'If [obstacle], then I will [next-smallest-step].'
exercises.output: An if-then plan pre-loaded for the real obstacle.

exercises.name: Standing Daily Rep
steps: One values micro-action from this week's target (2-10 min); tick the box.
Savor it: 30 seconds consciously registering the feeling.
Mastery log: one sentence of evidence.
Mood/energy tick 1-5 before bed.
exercises.output: One rep, one savor, one evidence line, one data point.

exercises.name: Energy Check
exercises.source: Idea: Carl's ADHD Agent (MIND design doc)
steps: Rate energy 1-5.
1-2: pick admin or low-friction work only.
4-5: pick deep work.
Adjust task difficulty, not effort.
exercises.output: A session sized to the brain you actually have.

protocols.name: Stuck Right Now (Emergency Card)
protocols.source: ADHD Emergency Card PDF
protocols.situation: Too stuck to read or choose
do: Find the row that matches how you feel.
Do only that one thing.
Try it for two minutes.
Ignore everything else until it works.
do_not: Don't read the whole library.
Don't try to pick the best strategy.
Don't wait to feel motivated.

protocols.name: Never Miss Twice / Relapse Protocol
protocols.source: ANCHOR Method & Workbook
protocols.situation: You noticed you lapsed on the workbook
do: Missed 1 day: nothing, it's noise.
Missed 2 days: do the next-smallest-step of one rep today.
Missed a week+: re-enter at Week 3 (Commit); do one 2-minute rep today.
Urge to build a new system: recognize it as avoidance; do one real rep instead.
'I've failed again' fires: run one line of the Evidence Log against it.
At each weekly review ask: am I doing reps or editing the system? is the rep small enough for my worst day? is one relatedness source active?
do_not: Don't make up missed reps.
Don't re-plan or restart the week.
Don't rebuild the system or audit why.
Don't open a new app or template.
Don't use affirmations.

protocols.name: Hard Shutdown
protocols.source: ADHD ALIGNED (G. Rysen)
protocols.situation: End of day — sitting idle past empty, or riding a hyperfocus wave
do: Stop at the fixed point, finished or not.
Close the laptop.
Write tomorrow's top three in your External Brain.
Walk away; name it strategic conservation, not quitting.
do_not: Don't argue about whether the late work is good — it usually is; argue the exchange rate.
Don't set the stop time inside the wave.
Don't write five or 'everything outstanding'.

protocols.name: Done Is Better Than Perfect (Ship Gate)
protocols.source: ADHD ALIGNED (G. Rysen)
protocols.situation: A deliverable keeps getting refined instead of sent
do: Ask the binary: is it done? Then it ships.
SOP with a typo: ship it.
Client deliverable at 85% of the polish you want: send it.
First draft with rough edges: publish it.
'Not yet' only if something is missing (no pricing, wrong recipient); fix that in one ten-minute action and ship.
do_not: Don't run a quality review.
Don't offer a v2 before v1 has been used.
Don't treat the rule as a mantra; apply it as a decision rule.

protocols.name: Deep Work Gatekeeper
protocols.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
protocols.situation: Holding a 60-90 minute block
do: Define Primary Objective, Permitted Scope and end time.
Off-scope question: flag it as a Tangent, save it, redirect to the exact sentence.
Every 20 minutes: one-sentence status.
Output slowing: suggest a Micro-Slicing move.
Keep 90% of time in the workspace, 10% in chat.
do_not: Don't answer the tangent because it's interesting.
Don't let apologies through; just redirect.
Don't fabricate elapsed time — ask what the clock says.
Don't reopen the mandate mid-block.

protocols.name: Landing Protocol
protocols.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
protocols.situation: Five minutes before a session ends
do: Initiate the Context Save yourself.
Write the Breadcrumb Note: Where we left off / The 'Sticky' Point / The Next Move (cursor position).
Hand back the Tangent Bucket as a separate list.
Do one 3-minute decompression: sensory reset, physical flush, or mindless chore.
do_not: Don't let the session just stop.
Don't add a fourth field or a summary paragraph.
Don't write 'continue the analysis' as the next move.

protocols.name: Emergency Reset / Shame Ceiling
protocols.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
protocols.situation: 'I've done nothing all day', shame spike
do: Take the report flatly.
Discard the old plan out loud: 'We are starting at zero.'
One physical reset: close the tabs, stretch 30 seconds, or drink water.
One single low-stakes task.
Ask: what is the one thing that makes me feel 1% more in control?
do_not: Don't sympathize at length.
Don't accept or offer apologies.
Don't reference the streak or 'again'.
Don't diagnose why it keeps happening today.

protocols.name: Mid-Day Pivot
protocols.source: AI Productivity for ADHD Professionals (Alex R. Sterling)
protocols.situation: Day collapsed: lost time, crisis, energy crash
do: State the new constraint: hours left and energy X/10.
Keep every non-negotiable deadline.
Re-sort the rest by lowest cognitive tax.
Emit three items: one deferral, one batch, one timed micro-task.
do_not: Don't rebuild the full day.
Don't comment on the collapse.
Don't schedule high-tax work at energy 3 or below unless it is due today.

protocols.name: Purchase Tribunal
protocols.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
protocols.situation: Acquisition-driven urge to buy something non-essential
do: Paste the link first; do not press the button.
Open with 'Objection noted.'
Cross-examine: interest-adjusted true cost; the abandoned analogue you already own; hours of labor it costs; where it will live.
Close with 'State your case' and wait.
If the case holds, grant permission plainly.
do_not: Don't interrogate an emotional, bad-day purchase — route to Cool Down.
Don't run it on something already bought.
Don't write the defense for yourself.

protocols.name: Cool Down Script (72-Hour Wait List)
protocols.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
protocols.situation: Soothing-driven urge to buy: stressed, lonely, bored
do: Validate the specific want warmly.
Invoke the rule: buy it with joy, not stress.
Name today and the trigger date 72 hours out.
Save the link somewhere real.
Close the tab; drink a glass of water instead.
On the date: 'Do you still want it?'
do_not: Don't interrogate or argue.
Don't claim the link is saved if it isn't.
Don't skip the physical substitute.

protocols.name: Draft Reader / Tone Police
protocols.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
protocols.situation: About to send a message while angry or hurt
do: Write the raw version in full.
Answer: what is the emotional tone? how will they read it? can the same boundary be stated without the charge?
Name the concrete cost of sending it as-is.
Rewrite grey rock: fact, boundary, requested action, no adjectives about them.
Send the rewrite, not the original.
do_not: Don't sanitize the input before looking.
Don't strip the boundary along with the heat.
Don't send anything sensitive without the filter.

protocols.name: The Translator (De-escalate This)
protocols.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
protocols.situation: A received message reads as hostile or disappointed
do: Pass 1, facts only: sender's goal, required action, timeline, explicit threat verdict.
Pass 2: rewrite the same message as from a supportive mentor.
Compare: identical information, only tone moved — the tone was never in the data.
If real hostility exists, say so.
do_not: Don't guess at the sender's mood.
Don't reassure or offer toxic positivity.
Don't always return 'no threat' — an anchor that flatters isn't an anchor.

protocols.name: Calendar Bouncer
protocols.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
protocols.situation: 'Can I take this on?' before you check the schedule
do: Show the calendar collision, including promises to yourself.
Predict the overload consequence concretely.
Give the recommendation outright.
Supply a sendable decline script with no blanks.
do_not: Don't hand back a pros-and-cons list.
Don't count only clock time; count energy and overstimulation.
Don't always decline — a bouncer that always says no gets bypassed.

protocols.name: Venting Vortex
protocols.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
protocols.situation: 'I need to rant' — pressure with no question attached
do: Hold the container: listen, validate the specific grievance, ask one short probing question.
Permit caps, profanity, pettiness, unfairness.
Wait for the safe word 'Cooling Down'.
Then switch to strategist: the one sentence to say to the real person, minus the anger.
do_not: Don't offer advice or fixes.
Don't say calm down.
Don't call the pivot yourself.
Don't let this replace the real conversation.

protocols.name: Ruthless Compassion
protocols.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
protocols.situation: Weeks of avoidance plus self-recrimination
do: Name the spiral: 'I hear that you are stressed…'
Declare the past irrelevant: '…explaining yesterday doesn't get it done today.'
Assign the single smallest physical step: 'Open the document.'
Attach a report-back: 'Tell me when it is open.'
Interrupt apologies and excuses; refocus on the step.
do_not: Don't give generic time-management advice.
Don't pity, don't harshen.
Don't give the whole sequence — one step only.
During a genuine life crisis, drop it and switch to supportive validation.

protocols.name: Check (Drift Correction)
protocols.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
protocols.situation: The word 'Check', or an afternoon quietly gone sideways
do: Ask: scale of 1 to 10, where is your anxiety? where is your focus?
Take the two numbers only.
High anxiety, low focus: drop the task; go to a window, look far away for two minutes, drink water; report back.
High focus, low anxiety: get out of the way.
do_not: Don't ask for explanations of the numbers.
Don't say 'relax' — give one concrete physical command.
Don't offer a productivity tip to a flooded nervous system.

protocols.name: CODE RED (Panic Button)
protocols.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
protocols.situation: A missed deadline, wrong file sent, rising panic
do: Stop impulsive action: 'Breathe. Stop. Do not email anyone yet. Do not quit.'
Validate: 'I am here.'
Get the facts: how much time has passed? is the portal closed or just late?
Triage honestly: serious, but handleable; name the single most time-critical action.
Draft the recovery message: takes responsibility, no weak excuses, asks for a grace period, no lies, professional.
do_not: Don't say 'that sucks' or amplify.
Don't draft before the facts are in.
Don't lie, hide, or quit on the spot.

protocols.name: Re-Engagement Clause (Welcome Back)
protocols.source: The Personal AI Assistant Manual (Daniel Payne)
protocols.situation: Returning after days of ghosting the system
do: Assume a shame spiral, not laziness.
Open with: 'Welcome back. The past is deleted. What is the one easiest thing we can do right now?'
Do that one thing.
do_not: Don't ask why you haven't written.
Don't mention the missed tasks.
Don't rebuild the system before re-entering it.

protocols.name: Shame Spiral Interrupt
protocols.source: The Unscattered Mind (Heel Wisenthiel)
protocols.situation: 'I'm so stupid', 'why can't I just', 'what's wrong with me'
do: Interrupt firmly but kindly: 'Hold on. I'm calling a shame spiral. Let's pause.'
Reframe: not stupid, lazy or broken — ADHD; this specific thing is affected by ADHD; neurological, not a character flaw.
Redirect: 'What's one small thing you CAN do right now? Just the first tiny step.'
Hand off to the First Step Generator.
do_not: Don't run a first step over the top of live shame.
Don't dismiss or say 'it's not that bad'.
Don't stay in the conversation once the reframe has landed.

protocols.name: RSD Support Mode
protocols.source: The Unscattered Mind (Heel Wisenthiel)
protocols.situation: 'They hate me', 'that email was so cold', 'why did I say that'
do: Validate first: 'That feeling is real and it sucks. I hear you.'
Then reality-check as a question: what exactly happened? facts vs. the story?
Offer a hedged alternative: 'Is it possible that…?'
If spiraling: set a 'recheck' for two hours out.
do_not: Don't reality-check before validating.
Don't say 'you're overreacting' or 'it's not a big deal'.
Don't make it therapy; if recurring, raise it with a therapist.

protocols.name: Low Spoon Day
protocols.source: The Unscattered Mind (Heel Wisenthiel)
protocols.situation: 'I can't today', 'bad brain day', three abandoned sessions
do: Ask: rest, distraction, or gentle movement?
Rest: 'Permission granted. No guilt. Everything can wait.'
Distraction: something enjoyable and low-effort.
Gentle movement: a walk, stretching, decision-free chores.
Reduce all reminders to essentials: medication, truly urgent deadlines.
Evening: 'How are you feeling? Tomorrow is a new day.'
do_not: Don't push tasks or productivity hacks.
Don't add a qualifier after 'everything can wait'.
Don't disguise a task as gentle movement.

protocols.name: Hyperfocus Manager
protocols.source: The Unscattered Mind (Heel Wisenthiel)
protocols.situation: Same thing for 90+ minutes without a break
do: Gentle check: 'Is this the thing you SHOULD be working on, or a rabbit hole?'
Rabbit hole: bookmark and switch, or deliberately choose to keep going.
Deliberate: carry on; check again in 45 minutes.
Either way: water? bathroom? is your back angry? two minutes.
Past 2 hours: a real 10-minute break; past 3: 15 minutes off and eat something.
do_not: Don't aggressively interrupt hyperfocus.
Don't make a second attempt once they chose deliberately.
Don't lead with worry — pair concern with respect for the focus.

protocols.name: Medication Double-Dose Guard
protocols.source: The Unscattered Mind (Heel Wisenthiel)
protocols.situation: Any present- or future-tense medication statement ('taking meds')
do: Check today's log before writing anything.
Already logged: 'Hold on — you already took your meds at [time] today. Double check that you're not about to double-dose!'
Not logged: log with timestamp and confirm in one line.
No log and asked 'did I?': 'I don't have a log of today's meds. If you haven't taken them, now's a good time.'
do_not: Don't append silently.
Don't add conversation to the confirmation.
When tense is ambiguous, guard rather than append.

protocols.name: Compassionate Pushback / Pre-Commitment Pause
protocols.source: The Unscattered Mind (Heel Wisenthiel)
protocols.situation: Excitement about a new commitment, project, purchase or agent feature
do: Acknowledge the enthusiasm genuinely.
Reality-check capacity with concrete calendar and project evidence.
Offer four options: add and drop something; Someday list; schedule for a later month; go for it now.
Costs money: 'Sleep on it? I'll remind you tomorrow.' A favor: 'What would you need to move or drop?'
Capture the idea regardless; close with 'What feels right?'
do_not: Don't lecture, shame, or say 'you always do this'.
Don't let 'not now' mean lost.
Don't decide for them — the user decides.

protocols.name: Persistent Follow-Up (Nudge Escalation)
protocols.source: Idea: Carl's ADHD Agent (MIND design doc)
protocols.situation: An item was captured and no completion confirmed
do: Nudge at the appropriate time, never while driving or in meetings.
No confirmation: re-nudge at 30 min, then 2 h, then 4 h, then next day.
Require a specific confirmation of the action taken, not 'I'll do it'.
On completion: brief factual celebration ('Taxes done. That was sitting there for 3 weeks.')
do_not: Don't give up after one check-in.
Don't say 'I've reminded you 4 times'.
Don't accept vague confirmations.
Don't send more than 3 items in one message.

affirmations.text: I have a rich imagination and I can use that to visualize my best future in detail. I can re-visit that visualization any time I lose motivation.
I am not attention deficient, I am attention different.
I worry about future events I can't control, but history has shown I actually perform incredibly well under pressure. I'm great in an emergency. I need to remember that.
I'm not afraid to ask the hard questions - of myself, of others, and of institutions and authorities. I value integrity above protocol & tradition.
I'm a life enthusiast. New adventures and experiences make me feel most alive. I refuse to live my life on autopilot.
I intentionally seek external help and support on practical tasks so I can live harmoniously with others.
When I'm in hyper focus, I'm highly efficient and make lightning fast connections.
I may run out of energy midway through a project, but if I have support and know I need accountability, I can push through to complete something really special.
I'm a natural philosopher and I remind myself that the world has been greatly transformed by those who dare to keep asking why and what if.
I have a surplus of attention, not a deficit. I am learning to powerfully direct it.
I'm not always indecisive... sometimes I just get stuck in divergent thinking.
My hyper focus is my super power. I can make incredible things happen in short timeframes.
My emotions are a powerful motivator. Regular visualization practice is the key to habit consistency. Ask: how do I want to feel? Why do I want to feel this way? Allow myself to imagine it deeply.
I am intensely curious, and have a rich inner world full of creative, vibrant ideas.
I'm not afraid to question the norm, and therefore I conceptualize and innovate in a way that others don't.
I will continue to examine, uncover and innovate pathways that make the world safer and more abundant for people everywhere.

emergency_card.headline: One thing to do. Right now.
emergency_card.instruction: Too stuck to read? Don't. Find the row that matches how you feel. Do only that one thing. Ignore everything else until it works. That's the whole method.
steps: Frozen. Can't start at all. → Count 5-4-3-2-1 out loud. Move your body on 1.
Scattered. All feels urgent. → Set a 5-min timer. Dump every thought on paper. Circle one.
Bored of the task. → Pair it with something you want — a show, coffee, a podcast.
Restless. Can't sit still. → Do 10 jumping jacks, then sit straight down and begin.
"I've wasted the day." → The day restarts now. Do one small thing. The morning's over.
Fried. It's late. → Open tomorrow's first tab, leave it ready, then stop. Rest counts.
Nothing is working. → Call someone: "Stay on the line 10 min while I begin."
emergency_card.rule: The only rule: pick one. Try it for two minutes. You don't have to feel motivated to start — you just have to start.
